stories.title: Rare piglet the size of 'a grapefruit with legs' born at zoo
stories.summary: Rana's arrival is described as a "lifeline for the species", which is in rapid decline in the wild.
stories.post: 📰 NEWS: Rare piglet the size of 'a grapefruit with legs' born at zoo. Rana's arrival is described as a "lifeline for the species", which is in rapid decline in the wild. Source: BBC Science.
article_sentences: An endangered piglet the size of a "grapefruit with legs" when she was born has made her debut at Chester Zoo, conservationists have said.
Rana - a babirusa known as a "pig-deer" - has been described as a "lifeline for the species" which is in rapid decline in the wild.
Babirusas in the wild are found on just four Indonesian islands and the zoo said they were being wiped out due to African swine fever reaching the islands five years ago.
The attraction's Hannah Owens said Rana was "tiny" when she was born but has "grown a lot and is doing really well".

Until recently, babirusas were considered vulnerable to extinction by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature, external, but are due to be upgraded to "critically endangered", the zoo said.
Rana is the fifth piglet born to mother Matano, who was herself born at Chester Zoo 11 years ago and now has descendants living in zoos across Europe.
Owens said while babirusas "are doing well in our care" numbers in the wild were "radically reducing" and it would be "horrendous if they disappeared, because they were amazing, charismatic animals".
She added: "Piglets like Rana are a lifeline for the species."
Unlike most pigs, babirusas typically have just one or two offspring at a time rather than large litters - one reason their numbers recover slowly when wild populations are hit hard.
New mothers are also highly sensitive to disturbance, so keepers kept an eye on Rana and Matano remotely via a baby monitor until the pair were ready to be seen in public.
Owens said babirusa meant "pig-deer" in Malay because of their distinctive look.
"They're much less hairy than other pigs - Rana had ginger fuzz when she was born, but that's gone now," she said.

stories.title: East's astronomers plan for solar eclipse
stories.summary: Watch parties, pinhole cameras, colanders - experts offer tips on Wednesday's celestial event.
stories.post: 📰 NEWS: East's astronomers plan for solar eclipse. Watch parties, pinhole cameras, colanders - experts offer tips on Wednesday's celestial event. Source: BBC Science.
article_sentences: Cambridge has been facing an "astronomer exodus" this summer as they have travelled abroad to see Wednesday evening's total solar eclipse, according to an astrophysicist.
Dr Matt Bothwell, from Cambridge University's Institute of Astronomy, is among many stargazers heading to northern Spain, which is due to experience the full blackout on Wednesday evening.

Meanwhile, Jonathan Clough, vice chairman of the Cambridge Astronomical Association, is heading north on a cruise to the Faroe Islands in the hope of seeing the total eclipse, the Northern Lights and the Perseid meteor shower all at once.
Watch parties take place across the East of England, which will experience a partial eclipse, but one which will have the greatest coverage of the Sun since 1999.
Aston is hosting a watch party for many of his neighbours in a dark corner of his housing estate in Northampton.
The 14-year-old is a junior ambassador for the charity UK Astronomy, to which he donates the proceeds from his book.
All About Space.
"I'm going to take two telescopes, some equipment and offer experiences for all ages.
UK Astronomy has donated loads of solar glasses," he said.
While he has seen three previous eclipses "every single one is different, especially this one as it is the biggest solar eclipse to hit the UK until 2090," he added.
"And just after the sun sets, the Perseid meteor shower will peak and the sky will be incredibly dark with 50 to 100 meteors every hour."
Where can you watch it?
